EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

--------------------------------------------------  
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  

Strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension on a propensity-score–matched sample of banks that applied for CPP capital.  

Why appropriate?  
• “Treatment” (capital injection) happened at a well-defined date for each recipient bank.  
• Non-recipient applicant banks provide a natural comparison group—they faced the same macro shock, filed similar paperwork, and were evaluated under the same CPP guidelines but did not obtain funds.  
• Loan-level HMDA observations can be aggregated to the bank-quarter (or bank-year) level, allowing bank and time fixed effects.  
• Event-study coefficients (leads/lags) let us test the parallel-trends assumption and measure dynamic effects.  

--------------------------------------------------  
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  

Treatment variable  
TREAT_i = 1 if bank i received CPP capital; 0 otherwise.  

Treatment timing  
POST_it = 1 for all quarters t ≥ the quarter in which bank i’s CPP funds were disbursed (first Treasury transaction date).  
Leads and lags at the quarterly frequency, k = −8,…,+8.  

Control group  
Non-recipient banks that (i) filed an application to CPP but (ii) were not accepted or withdrew, matched to recipients by a one-to-one nearest-neighbor propensity score (calculated on 2006–Q3 2008 averages of size, Tier-1 ratio, ROA, NPL ratio, deposit growth, and geography).  

Unit of observation  
Bank × quarter. Risk measures are loan-amount-weighted averages of HMDA originations in the quarter.  

(There is no running variable or cutoff; the design is not RDD.)  

--------------------------------------------------  
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  

A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of treatment, recipient and matched non-recipient banks would have followed the same evolution in mortgage-risk metrics after 2008:Q4.  
Plausibility: Both groups applied and were evaluated under CPP; pre-crisis performance variables used in matching increase plausibility. We will show statistically indistinguishable pre-treatment trends in the event-study.  

A2. No anticipation: Banks could not materially change mortgage composition prior to knowing they would receive CPP capital (decision announcements were often only weeks before disbursement).  
Plausible because approval information was private until Treasury press releases right before funding; we still test for “−1” and “−2” leads.  

A3. Stable composition: Entry/exit of banks or mergers do not differentially affect the groups post-treatment.  
Mostly plausible; we will drop banks acquired within 12 months of treatment and perform a “leave-one-out” robustness.  

A4. No spillovers: A recipient’s ability to expand risk taking does not mechanically force non-recipients in the same local market to adjust their risk in the opposite direction.  
Less certain; we will add county-year fixed effects and look at within-county comparisons as a robustness.  

--------------------------------------------------  
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATIONS  

T1. Time-varying unobservables correlated with approval (e.g., regulators may have had soft information on pending losses).  
Mitigation:  
• Include bank-specific linear trends.  
• Include quarterly financial controls (Tier-1 ratio, NPL, ROA) interacted with time.  
• Conduct a falsification test on credit-card loans whose underwriting is less politically salient.  

T2. Credit-demand shocks that differ across banks (e.g., county-level house-price collapses).  
Mitigation:  
• Merge Zillow/Case-Shiller county price indices; include county×quarter fixed effects or an interacted county-trend.  
• Triple-D design: Compare risk of mortgages that each bank originates inside vs. outside its home state.  

T3. Survivorship bias (weaker non-recipients may fail, biasing control group risk downward).  
Mitigation:  
• Use intent-to-treat definition; keep failed banks through the quarter before failure, assign missing outcomes to last observed value (“last observation carried forward”) and show robustness to dropping failed banks.  

--------------------------------------------------  
5. R CODE OUTLINE  

```r
# Load required packages
library(data.table)   # fast merge
library(fixest)       # high-dim FE regressions
library(MatchIt)      # propensity score matching
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Data loading ----------------------------------------------------------
hmda  <- fread("hmda_2006_2010.csv")        # loan-level
tarp  <- fread("tarp_transactions.csv")     # bank-level
y9c   <- fread("fr_y9c_quarterly.csv")      # bank-quarter

# 2. Construct bank-quarter risk measures ----------------------------------
# Example: loan-value-ratio (LTV) and high-risk indicator
hmda[, high_ltv := as.integer(ltv_ratio > 0.9)]
hmda_q <- hmda[, .(
      avg_ltv   = weighted.mean(ltv_ratio, loan_amount, na.rm = TRUE),
      share_hi  = weighted.mean(high_ltv , loan_amount, na.rm = TRUE),
      n_loans   = .N
), by = .(fdic_id, quarter)]

# 3. Merge with bank data ---------------------------------------------------
tarp[, treat := 1L]
tarp[, treat_date := as.IDate(transaction_date)]
y9c[, quarter := as.yearqtr(date)]
setkey(hmda_q, fdic_id, quarter)
setkey(y9c,   fdic_id, quarter)
panel <- y9c[hmda_q]                       # inner join
panel <- merge(panel, tarp[,.(fdic_id, treat, treat_date)],
               by = "fdic_id", all.x = TRUE)

# Treatment timing
panel[, post := (quarter >= as.yearqtr(treat_date))]
panel[is.na(post), post := 0]
panel[is.na(treat), treat := 0]

# Event-study dummies k = −8,…,+8
for(k in -8:8){
  panel[, paste0("leadlag_",k) := as.integer( (quarter - as.yearqtr(treat_date)) == k )]
}
# Trim outside window
panel <- panel[rowSums(panel[, paste0("leadlag_", -8:8), with=F])==1 | treat==0]

# 4. Propensity score matching ---------------------------------------------
prevars <- c("tot_assets","tier1_cap","roa","npl_ratio","deposit_growth","region")
pre   <- unique(panel[quarter < as.yearqtr("2008 Q4"),
                      c("fdic_id", prevars), with=FALSE])
m.out <- matchit(treat ~ ., data = pre, method="nearest")
matched_ids <- data.table(fdic_id = rownames(m.out$match.matrix))
panel <- panel[fdic_id %in% matched_ids$fdic_id]

# 5. Main DID regression ----------------------------------------------------
did <- feols(avg_ltv ~ post*treat + bank_size + tier1_cap + roa,
             data = panel,
             fixef = ~ fdic_id + quarter,
             cluster = ~ fdic_id)
summary(did)

# 6. Event-study specification ---------------------------------------------
# Omit k = −1 as baseline
omit <- "leadlag_-1"
event <- feols(avg_ltv ~ i(leadlag, treat, ref = -1) + bank_size + tier1_cap,
               data = panel,
               fixef = ~ fdic_id + quarter,
               cluster = ~ fdic_id)
etable(event)

# 7. Robustness: placebo on 2007Q3 pseudo-treatment ------------------------
panel[, fake_post := (quarter >= as.yearqtr("2007 Q3"))]
placebo <- feols(avg_ltv ~ fake_post*treat + bank_size + tier1_cap,
                 data = panel[quarter < as.yearqtr("2008 Q4")],
                 fixef = ~ fdic_id + quarter,
                 cluster = ~ fdic_id)
summary(placebo)
```

--------------------------------------------------  
6. EXPECTED RESULTS  

Economic theory (moral hazard + political lending pressure) suggests CPP recipients may loosen underwriting standards. I expect:  

• Average LTV ratio ↑ by ≈ 2–3 percentage points (roughly a ½ standard deviation) after receipt.  
• Share of high-LTV (>90%) loans ↑ by 5–8 percent relative to matched controls.  
Direction: positive effect on risk measures. Magnitude moderate: enough to detect but not enough to fully offset CPP capital gains.  

--------------------------------------------------  
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (for DID)  

C1: Pre-treatment parallel trends documented  1  
C2: No differential anticipation (no pre-trend spikes) 1  
C3: No spillovers/contamination across groups   0  
C4: Stable group composition (minimal attrition)  1  
C5: Correctly clustered SEs & two-way FE specification 1  

Total = 4 / 5. I view the remaining threat (spillovers) as the most serious and will test/address it as described above.
